narrative:
Your application was denied because a predictive model evaluated your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and it placed you at a 52.7% probability of failing. In practical terms, the model saw you as slightly more likely to fail than to pass, which made admitting you too risky.

The most decisive factor in this outcome was your LSAT score. At 28.50, it sits far below the average of 37.18 among students whose applications were accepted. This single difference was the strongest force pushing the prediction toward failure, and it outweighed every other factor the model examined. Everything else in your file could not fully compensate for this gap.

Two other factors were important, and notably, both worked in your favor. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 is above the accepted-student average of 3.23, which nudged the prediction toward passing. Your first-year class standing also helped: you placed in the fifth decile, which is stronger than the accepted average of roughly the sixth decile. These two strengths signal that you have solid academic discipline and early law-school aptitude.

However, the combined pull of your GPA and class standing was too weak to offset the LSAT deficit. The denial was driven entirely by this academic pattern—not by your gender, race, or family income, which did not influence the decision at all.

What should you do next? Retake the LSAT with dedicated preparation. Even a moderate improvement would remove the single largest risk in your profile and likely tip the prediction in your favor. You might also consider a part-time program or additional first-year tutoring to further strengthen your recorded performance, but the clear and urgent priority is improving that score and reapplying.
